name: Carla Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What happens on an ordinary workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Carla Rossi, 43, building timber playground structures and doing general trades on new school sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of construction work, so ordinary frames are familiar, though I ask the lead about a new swing fitting. I use an AI app now and then for a drawing note, but I test the actual hardware. The contractor pays a typical site wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What supports the family at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a community library desk, answering visitors and booking rooms. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three months of expenses saved. There are some similar building jobs nearby, but I would rather stay with a crew that keeps children clear until every hanger is tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the playground crew that a tidier parts order would save us a trip, but the swing hanger still needs checking with a real pull. I use an AI app sometimes to explain a drawing note, then ask the site lead. The children who use the playground will not care how fast the office typed the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and can build the usual timber frame, with the lead checking an unfamiliar connection. We earn a normal site wage, my partner works at a community library desk, and we have about three months of expenses saved. The library might save time on routine questions, but neither of us expects fewer hours from this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid playground shifts and record the pull-test number for each swing hanger as the lead signs it. In the first year I'd use the AI app for odd plan notes, checking each answer against the approved sheet. We would continue our small automatic savings transfer from each payday while both hours stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, though I listen when the library talks about new screens. I like an order arriving complete. I care more about a safe swing than a faster email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the hanger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bolt had the right label but a bent thread, and the lead spotted it during fitting. We replaced it and logged the pull test before children came near the frame. A correct box label was not a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner do at the library?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner answers visitors, checks books in and helps book community rooms. The job is more than typing, but a lot of the questions are routine. We have not heard of any hours being cut, so I am not going to pretend the wage has gone.

say: I would say faster **parts orders** still need real swing-hanger tests.
I would remind coworkers the **children using the playground** need sound fittings.
think: I am a **certified experienced** worker on a typical site wage.
Three months saved and steady **library hours** make the mild picture manageable.
do: Keep paid **playground shifts** and record signed hanger pull tests.
Use **AI occasionally** for plan notes verified against approved sheets.
Continue automatic **savings transfers** while both wages stay steady.
feel: Mostly **calm**, while listening for changes to library work.
S0.quote: A correct box label was not a safety check.
fieldNote: Carla’s **bent bolt thread** explains her insistence on an actual pull test despite correct labels.
The library desk has **routine tasks**, but she has no evidence of lost hours in the plateau.

steps.text: Keep paid playground shifts and record signed swing-hanger pull tests
Use AI for occasional plan notes and verify approved drawings
Continue small automatic savings transfers while both wages remain steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the builder may order timber and book crews faster, which could help on site. The library desk at home also answers questions and books rooms, so I would ask my partner how its hours are changing. I would want the council and the contractor to tell workers what is being automated before a new roster appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still build the play structures, but my partner's library desk hours could shrink much sooner. Three months saved would carry a short gap, not a long mortgage on one wage. I am open to proven tools, yet a better timber order would not balance the household if the library cut shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the site lead to show me the digital timber list for one playground section and check it against the delivered beams. My partner would ask the library manager about planned hours. In the first year I'd keep paid site shifts, use AI to check unfamiliar materials notes, and bring any unfair roster changes to the workers' association meeting with actual payslips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the home wage, even while I can see the site benefit. A complete load would make our day easier. A half-empty library roster would make the evening budget harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take three payslips and the old and new rosters, not a story from the break room. My partner would decide whether to join me. We need to know if fewer routine questions really mean fewer paid desk hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the digital list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the lead shows it working on one section. I would check the beam labels against the drawing and count what arrives. I am happy to keep a useful tool, but I will not skip the pull test to save time.

say: I would welcome **faster timber orders** while asking about library desk hours.
I would seek clear **worker notice** before changed rosters appear.
think: My partner’s **library hours** could realistically shrink soon.
Three months saved will not carry a long **one-wage mortgage**.
do: Check one **digital timber list** against delivered beams.
Use **AI** for materials notes while keeping paid site shifts.
Take changed **rosters and payslips** to the workers’ association meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about library pay despite a possible site benefit.
S1.quote: A half-empty library roster would make the evening budget harder.
fieldNote: Carla names **library booking and answers** as the earliest household exposure, before site robots.
Her association plan relies on **three payslips and rosters**, while her tool adoption depends on a real one-section test.

steps.text: Keep paid playground shifts and check one delivered timber list
Use AI for materials notes and verify them against approved drawings
Take changed library rosters and payslips to the workers association meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew full thinking AI reaches library questions and room booking by 2028, while robots able to build playgrounds arrive around 2031. Our family cannot count those as one distant event. I would ask both employers for a written account of paid roles after each change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the library faces AGI and 48 when robots can do my hands-on carpentry. My partner's hours could fall first, and my site job could follow. Three months of savings give us some room to search, but both wages are needed for the mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my paid building shifts and ask the contractor for a supervised robot safety trial on a real play frame. My partner would apply for paid library community-program work if desk hours fall, while I would apply for the local school maintenance opening if posted. In the first year after 2028 we'd postpone the planned patio work and direct any extra site pay into the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have calls to make and a little time in the account, but the sequence is hard. A robot that can build a frame might also check a swing, so I cannot sell inspection as a magic refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why community programs at the library?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner already helps set up children’s reading afternoons and knows the families who come. A paid program role might exist, though AGI could plan activities too. My partner would ask about real shifts before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would school maintenance be protected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A capable robot could build and repair a school frame too. I would apply because it is paid work nearby and my certificate fits the present job notice. I would keep looking if the work changed.

say: I would tell coworkers **2028 library AI** precedes 2031 playground robots.
I would ask both employers for **written paid-role plans**.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach my carpentry, after possible library hour cuts.
Three months saved cannot support a long **two-wage gap**.
do: Keep paid **playground shifts** and request a supervised robot trial.
Apply for **school maintenance** if a paid opening is posted.
Postpone **patio work** and put extra site pay into emergency savings after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about two job dates, with some control and a limited cushion.
S2.quote: A robot that can build a frame might also check a swing, so I cannot sell inspection as a magic refuge.
fieldNote: Carla separates the **2028 desk risk** from the 2031 arrival of capable hands-on robots.
She does not claim **inspection or school maintenance** is permanently safe after full robot capability.

steps.text: Keep paid playground shifts and request a supervised robot safety trial
Apply for a paid local school maintenance opening if posted
Postpone planned patio work after the 2028 change
Put extra site pay into the emergency account while hours remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the library's thinking tasks change by 2031 and capable site robots reach playground work around 2034. Five years gives the council time to tell library staff what paid work remains. It also gives the contractor time to test machines on real frames with children kept away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I may have more carpentry behind me, but my partner's desk income could be hit then. At 51, robots could do the site work I know. The children will be older, and the mortgage may still be there; five years helps if we use the time to reduce it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building playgrounds and use AI now and then to unpack a new fastening note, checking it with the lead. My partner would ask the library about paid community-program shifts; I would ask the workers' association to get a written staffing timetable from the contractor. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply to school maintenance only if it still has paid vacancies and put overtime toward the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the next few years, because the desk change is farther away and our current hours are stable. The warning lets us make small moves. I would still worry when the library gives my partner a new roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a community-program role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask how many paid afternoons are scheduled, who runs them and whether the hours replace desk time. A pleasant title without a wage would not help our loan. I would not make the decision for my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the association now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The contractor already has safety meetings, so workers can ask for a trial timetable before rumours begin. I would bring the bent hanger bolt as an example of what a robot must catch. A real test would teach us more than a sales film.

say: I would ask for **library staffing plans** before 2031 and site trials before 2034.
I would insist on **real frame tests** with children kept clear.
think: My partner’s **desk income** may change when I am 48.
I would be **51** when robots could do my playground carpentry.
do: Keep paid **playground work** and verify occasional AI fastening notes.
Ask the **workers’ association** for a contractor staffing timetable.
Apply for **school maintenance** after 2031 if paid vacancies remain.
feel: **Uneasy** near term with stable hours, while watching the later library roster.
S3.quote: A pleasant title without a wage would not help our loan.
fieldNote: Carla leaves the **library role decision** with her partner and asks for paid hours rather than a title.
Her **bent hanger bolt** remains the practical test case for a future site robot.

steps.text: Keep paid playground shifts and check fastening notes with the lead
Use AI occasionally for fastening notes verified against approved drawings
Ask the workers association for a written contractor staffing timetable
Apply for paid school maintenance after 2031 if vacancies remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew library desk work changes by 2036 and capable playground robots arrive around 2039. A decade is time for the council and builder to offer honest training and real job numbers. I would still keep testing every hanger on the playground we are building now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can do the hands-on build. Our children will be grown, so school costs will change, and the mortgage could be smaller if both wages hold. I cannot assume a pension or that a community-program job survives full AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid playground work and check the pull-test log with the lead on each site. We would put a little extra toward the mortgage each year after keeping three months of expenses in savings. In the first year after 2036 my partner would seek paid library work if desk hours fall, and I would ask for a real robot trial before considering another building crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the near years. The longer warning gives our family time to adjust without cutting the children's activities today. I would still want actual paid roles named before either employer calls a transition complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 56 if the mortgage were low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A lower loan would make a smaller wage easier, but we still need income for ordinary life. I do not have a pension promised at 56.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning a useful craft or service and ask for paid practice, whatever work you choose. I do not know what jobs will be open when they are adults. I would rather show them how we plan than hand them a frightening guess.

say: I would seek **real job numbers** before 2036 library AI and 2039 robots.
I would keep **pull-testing hangers** on today’s playgrounds.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and perhaps a smaller mortgage.
I cannot assume a **pension** or permanent community-program work.
do: Keep paid **playground work** and verify each pull-test log.
Pay a little extra toward the **mortgage** after protecting three months of savings.
Ask for a **real robot trial** after 2036 while my partner checks library openings.
feel: Mostly **calm** near term, while wanting paid roles named for later changes.
S4.quote: A lower loan would make a smaller wage easier, but we still need income for ordinary life.
fieldNote: Carla expects **grown children** by 2039 and a possibly smaller mortgage, without claiming retirement security.
Her demand for **named paid roles** covers both the library and playground work at different dates.

steps.text: Keep paid playground shifts and verify each swing-hanger pull-test log
Pay extra toward the mortgage after retaining three months of savings
Watch a real site robot trial before changing building crews

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because library desk work could change in 2028 and capable robots reach playground construction around 2031. Written staffing plans from both employers, real paid openings and a supervised site trial would help. A family budget needs hours, not just new job titles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the pull-test log after a robot fits a swing. The box label was right on the bolt we found bent. Children need a real check, and workers need to know who is paid to do it.

headlineQuote: A family budget needs hours, not just new job titles.
portrait: Carla is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker with experienced, average skills building school playground structures.
Typical site pay, a **library-desk wage** and three months saved support two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** for plan notes, then checks approved drawings and swing hardware with a lead.
She watches **two job dates** and asks the workers’ association for paid-role plans and real safety trials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change library work first, then bring capable playground robots around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing plans**, real paid openings and supervised site trials would help protect both wages.
